name: Developmental Editing
title: Developmental Editing
answer: Developmental editing is the big-picture work on a manuscript before line editing or copyediting, covering structure, argument, narrative arc, character development, pacing, chapter order, audience, and overall completeness. It asks whether the book works as a whole, not whether each sentence is clean. In AI-assisted practice, the same scope applies, but the editor may also use tools to map themes, track entities, or test reader response. The work is common in fiction, nonfiction, memoir, and academic writing, and it often begins with a manuscript assessment and an editorial letter.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the manuscript file, usually in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or Scrivener, plus outlines, style sheets, story bibles, and version histories. Editors use comments, track changes, shared folders, and project management tools to keep revisions traceable. Among the 732 AI tools the site tracks, some writing assistants can summarize chapters, extract character lists, or flag inconsistencies, though they are aids rather than replacements for editorial judgment. A typical setup also includes a secure place to store unpublished text, because manuscripts are confidential until publication.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A developmental editor reads the full manuscript, takes notes on structure and pacing, and then interviews the author about intent, audience, and constraints. The editor maps the book's arc, checks whether each chapter earns its place, and writes an editorial letter that explains strengths, problems, and possible revisions. With AI support, the editor might generate chapter summaries, build a timeline, or query a model for repeated phrases and dropped threads, then verify every suggestion against the text. The author decides what to accept, and the editor helps sequence the revisions into a workable plan. Follow-up passes check whether the changes solved the original problems without creating new ones.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Developmental editing involves confidential unpublished material, so contracts usually cover confidentiality, scope, deadlines, and who owns the edited files. Copyright in the manuscript stays with the author unless a contract says otherwise, and editors need clear permission before putting text into third-party AI services that may retain or train on it. Provenance matters: notes, suggestions, and AI-generated summaries are often kept distinguishable from the author's own words, and disclosure practices vary by publisher. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 involving AI music services, which shows that creative AI rights questions are being tested in courts. Editors and authors typically check their agreements and publisher policies rather than assume a default rule.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Developmental editing is moving toward hybrid workflows where editors use AI for structural analysis, consistency checks, and reader simulation while keeping human judgment for voice, meaning, and taste. Publishers and authors are experimenting with AI-assisted outlines, chapter-level feedback, and automated sensitivity reads, though results vary in quality. The role of the developmental editor may shift toward curating AI output, asking better questions, and defending originality in a crowded market. As tools improve, the field will likely see more explicit disclosure norms and more granular provenance records for editorial changes. The core task remains the same: helping a manuscript become the book it is trying to be.
